articles.author: mara-voss
articles.title: Three punts, three different corrections
articles.dek: Michael Dorrill has every reason to examine Mossdeep’s failed possessions. The useful part is identifying what failed on each one.

body.text: Michael Dorrill can have his three punts. I want him to bring three different explanations to the meeting. Mossdeep beat Petalburg 55–0, threw seven touchdown passes and allowed one conversion in twelve third-down attempts. The three possessions ending with Adam Vinathorn on the field still deserve scrutiny. They deserve enough scrutiny that nobody gets away with calling all of them the same mistake.

Each of those possessions gained seven yards before the punt. That is a wonderfully irritating coincidence for a coach who wants every possession to end in the other end zone. It is also where the resemblance becomes less useful. The first began with a sack. The second reached third-and-three after two runs. The third reached third-and-two after two runs in opposite directions. If the correction is simply to demand more intensity, the meeting has accomplished very little.

I like Dorrill’s refusal to treat a comfortable lead as permission to stop coaching. The best version of that approach asks precise questions and expects precise answers. A player should leave knowing what to recognize, where to go and why the alternative failed. A coach should leave prepared to explain the call. Nobody improves because the volume in the room has been raised to match the winning margin.

“Three possessions, seven yards apiece,” Dorrill said. “Explain how we got there. Explain what we do better. Then we can discuss the plays everybody enjoyed.” There is enough enjoyment elsewhere in this game to occupy several evenings. Accel BeckhmJr caught all nine of his targets, five for touchdowns. Shawn Mareman ran for 103 yards. The work on the unsuccessful possessions can afford to be specific.
Start with the sack

The first punt possession began with 2:29 left in the first quarter. Kabutops sacked Dram Marino for six yards on first down. Marino then threw short left to Gronkaludon for ten. On third-and-seven, Mareman ran left for three, with Glalie making the tackle. Vinathorn punted fifty-one yards; Ninjulio Jones limited the return to two.

That sequence gives Dorrill several useful questions. The first concerns avoiding the negative opening play. The second concerns the third-down choice after the offense had recovered much of the lost ground. A three-yard gain can be useful in several situations. This one left Mossdeep short of the required distance and sent out the punter. The eventual score cannot supply the missing first down.

I cannot assign the sack to a particular blocker from the play description. I can ask the staff to review the protection and Marino’s available response, because the record establishes the sack and the resulting long down. I can also question what the left-side run was intended to accomplish against that situation. The review should compare the intended answer with the actual tackle, rather than pretending that the call became sound once Mossdeep scored another touchdown later.

Petalburg’s defense deserves its share of the sentence. Kabutops created the problem and Glalie finished the possession. Sometimes the opponent executes. Good review distinguishes an opponent winning a rep from a player misunderstanding his assignment. Dorrill’s demand for perfection is most valuable when it helps players make that distinction, because the practice correction will be different.
Two manageable third downs

Mossdeep opened the second half with Mareman running up the middle for one yard and then six. On third-and-three, Marino threw short right to Gronkaludon. Girafarig broke up the pass. Vinathorn’s fifty-two-yard punt followed. The offense had reached a manageable distance, chosen a short throw and encountered a defender who prevented the completion.

That is a different conversation from first-down sack avoidance. Gronkaludon had already caught a touchdown and finished with six receptions for sixty-one yards. His successful work does not exempt the route from examination; it does make a lazy declaration that the target cannot be trusted particularly foolish. Review the timing, the available separation and the defender’s intervention. Keep the discussion on the rep that actually occurred.

The fourth-quarter punt began with a three-yard Mareman run left and a four-yard run right. On third-and-two, Marino’s short-middle throw to Jones fell incomplete. The drive again ended with seven yards. This time the record does not name a breakup. That absence does not establish a dropped pass or a missed assignment, and I have no interest in inventing one because a coach wants somebody to answer a difficult question.

Jones caught two of five targets for forty-six yards across the game. Those totals make the passing connection worth examining, but five targets are not a complete explanation of a receiver’s afternoon. The proper follow-up is to examine the actual attempts. On this one, the offense had two yards to find and failed to complete the short throw. That is the fact to begin with.
Preserve the part that works

The three failed possessions belong beside the successful third downs. Mossdeep converted six of nine overall, scored eight touchdowns and committed no turnover. The defense supplied three interceptions and seven sacks. A coach can demand correction while preserving confidence in an offense that repeatedly executed at a high level. In fact, he should. Otherwise players learn that the review has no relationship to their work.

Mareman’s rushing production is a useful example. Seventeen carries produced 103 yards and a touchdown, with another score on his only reception. His runs helped create the two short third downs discussed above. Removing those successes from the conversation would produce a distorted account of how Mossdeep reached its passing opportunities. The problem on those possessions occurred after manageable distances had been created.

Canalave will not be impressed by an argument about whether fifty-five points should have been more. The Bulwark are 7–6 and have just been shut out by Sunyshore. Mossdeep’s task is to sustain the execution that keeps an opponent from finding a route back into the game. The next defense gets its own tackles, its own pressure and its own opportunities to interrupt a possession. Preparation has to account for those possibilities.

Dorrill’s players do not need to pretend the win was unsatisfying to understand the standard. They can enjoy BeckhmJr’s five touchdown catches and still review the third-down incompletions. They can credit the shutout and still work on protection. I would begin the offensive meeting with the first sack, the Girafarig breakup and the short-middle incompletion, and require a concrete answer for each. Three punts are plenty of material when someone actually studies them.

articles.author: ellis-quill
articles.title: A quarterback earns another useful assignment
articles.dek: Lavender and Cerulean found different ways to keep asking something manageable of their passers. Trust showed up in the next call.

body.text: Travis Scarboro was asked whether Frosmoth had done enough in Lavender’s 13–3 win over Azalea. “We won,” he said. When the question turned to the next quarterback decision, he added, “We’ll evaluate it.” Anyone hoping to leave with a dramatic declaration had chosen the wrong interview. Asking him about a particular possession was more productive.

“There were throws that kept us on the field,” Scarboro said. “There were possessions we need to finish better. Those are separate evaluations.” I prefer that answer to the sudden coronations that tend to follow a replacement quarterback’s victory. Frosmoth completed eighteen of thirty-four passes for 162 yards, one touchdown and no interceptions. He helped Lavender reach 8–5. He also has more work available than a simple winning record can describe.

Mr. Clanky’s reported recovery counter has reached zero. That is an availability development, and the next starting assignment remains a separate decision. Lavender can assess the alternatives without retroactively reducing Frosmoth’s contribution to a holding action. The Wails needed the football looked after, enough useful completions to support their defense, and a scoring drive when the game was still waiting for someone to take charge. He supplied those things.

I find the distinction useful because Cerulean spent the same week showing a more dramatic version of trust. The Tide beat Cinnabar 18–17 after a final touchdown drive and a successful two-point try. Their quarterback, Farigiraf, had to keep throwing after an unsuccessful play threatened to end the afternoon. Lavender and Cerulean won different games, but both gave their passers another clear assignment when the previous series had become frustrating.
Lavender’s modest requests

Lavender’s touchdown came on a nine-play, seventy-one-yard possession beginning with 4:47 left in the second quarter. Frosmoth finished it with a four-yard throw short right to Beedrill on second-and-two. The score was small in distance and large in consequence. Neither side had scored before it, and Azalea never reached the end zone afterward.

The Wails did not need to spend the rest of the game proving that every possession could resemble that one. They added a forty-five-yard field-goal drive after halftime and a sixty-six-yard field-goal drive in the fourth quarter. Just a cactus made both attempts, from thirty-nine and thirty-two yards, and his extra point. A quarterback’s useful work includes moving the team into range for somebody else to complete the job.

There is a limit to the comfort in that sentence. Lavender punted five times and converted four of eleven third downs. A team with postseason ambitions will want more than thirteen points often enough that the staff should continue asking hard questions. Yet demanding improvement is compatible with recognizing the practical help a passer has already provided. Frosmoth’s zero interceptions mattered in a game where one touchdown was the difference between the two offenses.

Scarboro’s defense allowed Azalea one conversion in ten third-down attempts. That gave the offense repeated chances to find enough points. It also gave the coaches a reason to value ball security without treating caution as a complete offensive plan. Lavender still had to advance the ball. The long fourth-quarter possession, thirteen plays and nearly three minutes, was substantial work even though it ended in a field goal.
Cerulean asks again

Farigiraf’s situation at Cerulean was less forgiving. The Tide trailed 17–10 when their last touchdown possession began with 1:45 remaining. At 1:39, Gumshoos sacked him on third-and-two. A few seconds later, on fourth-and-ten, Farigiraf found number 35 Watchog deep right for nineteen yards. Cerulean had asked its quarterback to rescue the possession immediately after the sack, and he did.

“I thought they might be tired of seeing us by then,” Farigiraf said. “We decided to stay a little longer.” There was a playful edge to the answer, but very little spare time in the drive. Arctozolt gained seventeen on third-and-eight. Prinplup then became a repeated target on the right, catching passes for six, six, eight and fifteen yards during the possession. Farigiraf kept finding a way to give the next player something useful to do.

Prinplup caught all four of his targets for thirty-five yards. Asked about being called on so often at the end, he said, “Four passes, four catches. I’m happy to discuss which part was confusing.” There is a pleasing directness to that sort of receiver confidence. It gives a quarterback somewhere to look while everyone else is calculating how much time remains.

Number 35 Watchog caught the four-yard touchdown, and Farigiraf found Arctozolt short right for the two-point conversion. The Tide moved ahead 18–17. Cinnabar still reached a fifty-four-yard field-goal attempt, which missed wide left. Cerulean’s victory required its own late execution and one final unsuccessful kick by the opposition; both belong in the account.
Keep the praise specific

I would resist turning either result into a grand verdict on quarterback identity. Frosmoth’s next role is still a coaching decision. Farigiraf’s two touchdown passes did not erase six Cerulean punts or a blocked punt returned for a Cinnabar touchdown. Both teams had enough uneven possessions to keep the review busy. The performances became valuable through particular responses to those difficulties.

For Lavender, the praise can begin with the seventy-one-yard touchdown drive, the absence of interceptions and the fourth-quarter advance into field-goal range. For Cerulean, it can begin with the fourth-and-ten conversion and continue through the repeated completions to Prinplup. Those descriptions give players something they can recognize and attempt again. A vague announcement that a quarterback has finally become a winner gives him much less practical help.

The two clubs also carry different pressures into next week. Lavender hosts Celadon from a position of relative strength at 8–5. Cerulean visits Azalea at 6–7, with every result carrying weight in its effort to remain among the conference’s postseason contenders. Neither has earned the luxury of treating a good final score as the end of the evaluation.

I would like Scarboro to keep asking Frosmoth questions about the actual throws. I would like Cerulean to remember that number 35 Watchog’s nineteen-yard catch came immediately after a sack, with the game nearly gone. A passer can be corrected and still receive the next important assignment. Farigiraf got one on fourth-and-ten; Lavender’s staff has its own set of decisions to make before Celadon arrives.

articles.author: dorian-pike
articles.title: Crasher Wake, give that defense another touchdown
articles.dek: Pastoria sacked Eterna seven times and won 10–3. A team that can do that deserves more reliable help from its own offense.

body.text: Crasher Wake, I watched your defense sack the opposing quarterback seven times. I watched your offense finish with ten points. I am prepared to compliment one of those performances at considerable length, and I am prepared to ask the other side of the ball why the celebration needed to remain so nervous for so long.

Pastoria beat Eterna 10–3 and moved to 6–7. That is a useful win over a division leader, earned through a defense that repeatedly made the next passing down more difficult. The Waves have a reason to keep talking about the postseason. They also have a responsibility to make better use of the possessions their defense is buying. Seven sacks should purchase a little breathing room.

The winning touchdown drive finally arrived in the fourth quarter. Togekiss threw for 181 yards and one score without an interception. Farigiraf caught six passes for sixty-two yards, including the six-yard touchdown. Kilowattrel added sixty-one yards on three receptions. Those are real contributions, and I will name them before anybody accuses me of ignoring the offense entirely. I am asking for more because the useful pieces were visible.

Pastoria finished with 234 total yards. The rushing attack produced fifty-three on twenty-three attempts. Watchog carried eighteen times for forty-five yards. The Waves converted four of ten third downs and punted four times. An offense can win a particular game with those figures, as Pastoria has kindly demonstrated. Depending on that level of production every week gives the defense a very expensive assignment.
The defense created the opening

At the beginning of the fourth quarter, the opposing quarterback was sacked on consecutive plays. Aggron took him down for seven yards, and Krookodile followed with another seven-yard sack. Rapidash then returned the punt twenty-one yards. Pastoria’s next possession began with a chance to travel forty-three yards for the lead. The defense and return game had supplied an excellent invitation.

The first two offensive plays gained nothing. Watchog was stopped up the middle, and a deep-left pass intended for Seviper fell incomplete. Then Togekiss found Kilowattrel deep right for twenty-seven yards on third-and-ten. There is the play I want the coaching staff to spend time on. The Waves needed a substantial gain, and the quarterback and receiver supplied one at the exact moment the possession was threatening to become another punt.

Kilowattrel later gained eleven on a short-left throw. Farigiraf finished the drive with a six-yard touchdown reception short right at 4:06. Horsea’s extra point made it 10–3. That six-play possession contained different depths, different targets and enough completion value to overcome the empty opening snaps. Pastoria should investigate how to make those elements available earlier in games.

“I want the next one faster,” Togekiss said. “We had the chances. I’m already thinking about where we can get the ball out and keep moving.” That is an answer I appreciate from a quarterback. He can enjoy the victory and remain impatient with the possessions that made it difficult. Nobody is demanding an apology for winning. I am demanding that the next week’s preparation acknowledge how much work the defense performed.
The closeout still needed rescue

After taking the lead, Pastoria had an opportunity to improve its position with another possession. Three Watchog runs produced no gain, no gain and a one-yard loss. Horsea punted. The Waves handed their defense another one-score situation with the game still available to the opponent. A unit that had already supplied so much now had to finish the argument itself.

The defense did. Drednaw sacked the quarterback for seven yards on third-and-ten with 1:10 remaining. Nidorina then broke up the fourth-and-seventeen throw. Pastoria regained possession, and Watchog eventually supplied an eleven-yard run before the closing kneel. The last necessary rushing gain arrived. I would have preferred one on the previous possession, when three unsuccessful attempts made the defense go back out.

That does not require deciding that every run was a bad call. It requires asking what the offense can reasonably expect from a sequence of calls in that situation. Pastoria had just scored by completing meaningful passes, including a third-and-ten conversion. Its next series gained minus one yard on the ground. The coaches should examine the available alternatives with more care than a general instruction to protect the lead.

Farigiraf had a suitably mischievous answer when asked about his touchdown. “I thought seven points might improve the mood,” he said. It did. The receiver caught six of eight targets and gave Togekiss a useful presence throughout the game. Kilowattrel, quieter about his own work, said, “I knew the third down mattered. I wanted the catch to be the part people remembered.” Pastoria has enough material for an offensive review that includes successful answers.
Ten points should be the beginning

The Waves have scored 144 points in thirteen games and allowed 190. Those season totals explain why one efficient fourth-quarter drive should be treated as something to build from. The defense has just shown it can produce a game worthy of a contender. The offense has to make that performance less dependent on repeatedly winning the final difficult down.

Horsea contributed a fifty-yard field goal in the second quarter and the extra point after the touchdown. Pastoria’s scoring depended on a long kick and a single touchdown drive. I admire a kicker who does his job from fifty. I would also like the rest of the offense to give him more routine extra-point work. An accurate long field goal is valuable; needing one to account for most of the first three quarters is a demanding arrangement.

Petalburg visits next after being shut out at Mossdeep. Pastoria should expect a Pride team with a great deal to correct and every reason to want an immediate response. The Waves have their own clear assignment: turn more of their productive completions into sustained scoring possessions. They cannot assume that another opponent will remain stuck on three points while they search for their second score.

Crasher Wake can begin that preparation with the twenty-seven-yard completion to Kilowattrel, the eleven-yard follow-up and Farigiraf’s touchdown. He can place those plays beside the three-run possession that followed and ask which choices give his offense the best chance to stay on the field. The defense has delivered its evidence. Pastoria’s next scoring drive needs to arrive before the fourth quarter requires another rescue.
